framework.name: ISO/IEC 27001
framework.summary: International standard for running an information security management system. Its Annex A lists 93 reference controls that you choose from after assessing your risks. Relevant to any organisation seeking certification or a structured security programme.

requirements.title: Everyone can find the current, leadership-backed security ground rules and has confirmed reading them.
Everyone knows which security tasks they own and who is accountable.
No single person can both perform and approve a sensitive task alone.
Line managers set the example and hold their teams to security expectations.
When regulators, police or emergency services must be involved, the right contacts are already known.
The security team swaps early warnings and know-how with trusted peers in its industry.
Up-to-date knowledge of likely attackers and their methods shapes day-to-day defences.
Every project considers security risks from the start through to delivery.
Everything worth protecting, from databases to laptops, is recorded with a named owner.
Staff know what they may and may not do with company information and equipment.
Anyone leaving or changing role gives back laptops, badges and files before access ends.
A simple scheme ranks information by the harm its exposure, alteration or loss would cause.
Sensitive information carries a visible marker that tells people how to handle it.
Data shared by email, file transfer or courier, internally or externally, cannot be intercepted or misdirected.
Who gets into which buildings, data and applications follows need-to-know and least privilege.
Every account traces back to one real person or system, and orphaned accounts are removed.
Passwords, tokens and keys are handed out securely, and users know how to guard them.
Joiners, movers and leavers have permissions adjusted promptly, and stale rights are regularly pruned.
Before relying on a vendor, the organisation weighs what could go wrong and sets safeguards.
Vendor contracts leave no doubt about what protection the supplier must deliver.
Hardware, software and services bought in come from trustworthy, risk-assessed sources.
Vendors stay held to their security commitments, and their service changes never arrive unannounced.
Each cloud provider is vetted, its shared-responsibility split is clear, and leaving it is planned.
Before anything goes wrong, the incident team, its playbooks and escalation contacts are in place.
Each reported warning sign is triaged to decide whether it counts as an incident.
When an incident hits, the team contains it, removes the cause and restores normal service.
After each incident, root causes are reviewed and safeguards adjusted so it does not recur.
Proof relating to an incident is secured so it can support legal or disciplinary action.
Even in a crisis or outage, safeguards are not dropped to keep the business going.
IT services can be restored within the times the business needs after an outage.
Every legal and customer obligation touching security is tracked, owned and kept current.
Software licences, copyrights, trademarks and patents belonging to others are respected.
Important business files survive intact and unaltered for as long as they must be retained.
Duties owed to people whose details the organisation holds are mapped and honoured daily.
An assessor independent of the security function audits how protection is actually run.
Spot checks and self-assessments reveal where departments drift from the organisation's own requirements.
Step-by-step runbooks for day-to-day IT tasks are available to whoever performs them.
People are vetted before joining and again over time, scaled to role and risk.
Every hire signs up to clear protection obligations, matched by commitments from the organisation.
Everyone gets security know-how matched to their job, refreshed as the threat picture evolves.
Breaking security policy has clear, proportionate consequences that everyone knows in advance.
People who move on remain bound by duties that outlast their job, such as secrecy.
Staff, contractors and partners commit in writing to keep what they learn private.
Home and travelling workers use safeguarded connections, devices and workspaces.
Anyone who spots something odd knows exactly who to tell, and tells them fast.
Fences, walls and controlled doors mark where public space ends and protected space begins.
Doors to restricted spaces open only for people with permission, and every entry is logged.
Buildings and internal spaces are physically hardened so outsiders cannot simply walk in.
Cameras, alarms or guards detect anyone getting into buildings without permission.
Fire, flood, storms and deliberate physical attack cannot easily knock out facilities.
Extra rules apply to anyone spending time in high-security zones.
Papers are locked away and unattended computers locked so nothing sensitive is on show.
Servers and devices sit where theft, damage and prying eyes are least likely.
Equipment taken home or to clients is guarded against theft, loss and snooping.
Every data-carrying item, from USB stick to backup tape, is tracked until safely destroyed.
Generators, UPS units and resilient cooling keep systems up when building services fail.
Cable routes are concealed and shielded, so a single cut or tap cannot compromise operations.
Devices get scheduled upkeep by qualified people, so they keep working and data stays safe.
Before any device is scrapped or passed on, someone confirms nothing sensitive remains on it.
Staff laptops, phones and tablets are locked down, encrypted and managed wherever they are used.
Admin accounts are few, individually approved, separate from everyday logins and reviewed often.
Each user sees only the data their job justifies, enforced by the systems themselves.
Code repositories and pipelines are open only to the developers and services that need them.
Sign-in strength, such as MFA, rises with how much damage a stolen account could do.
Systems never run out of processing power, storage or bandwidth as the business grows.
Viruses and ransomware are stopped by tooling, backed by staff who recognise warning signs.
Known software flaws are patched or mitigated before attackers can exploit them.
Servers, devices and cloud services run hardened baselines, and unapproved drift is caught.
Data that has served its purpose is reliably destroyed wherever it is held.
Sensitive data is hidden or disguised wherever full values are not needed.
Unauthorised outflows of confidential data, by email, upload or USB, are spotted and stopped.
Recovery points exist for everything that matters, and restores are proven to work in practice.
Duplicate capacity keeps essential IT running if one component fails.
Systems leave a tamper-resistant trail that investigators and monitoring can rely on.
Suspicious activity across the estate is spotted early and investigated as a possible incident.
Every server and device shows the same correct time, so event timelines line up.
Tools that could sidestep built-in protections are available only to approved staff, case by case.
Only approved software can be put onto live production systems.
Routers, switches and firewalls are hardened and administered so traffic cannot be tampered with.
Internet links and network providers deliver the safeguards and uptime the organisation has specified.
Network zones stop a breach in one area from spreading freely to the rest.
Staff browsing is screened so dangerous or forbidden sites never load.
Strong, approved encryption protects data, and its secret keys are generated, stored and retired safely.
Engineering teams follow a defined method that weaves protection into planning, coding, testing and release.
Every new or purchased app has signed-off protection criteria before work begins.
Architects apply an agreed playbook of defensive patterns, like least privilege and defence in depth.
Programmers write code that avoids common weaknesses and resists attack.
New and changed systems must pass protection checks before they go live.
Contracted developers work to set expectations, and their code is checked before acceptance.
Work in progress cannot affect live systems because build and trial areas are kept apart.
Every alteration to live technology is assessed, authorised, tested and logged before release.
Test environments use made-up or masked data, never raw customer records without safeguards.
Reviewers and management agree scope and timing in advance, so inspections never disrupt production.
